paras: The reported cow-carcass punishment in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana, was an incident described in late summer 1881 in which unnamed men were said to have sewn a Black man accused of cow theft inside the carcass of a disemboweled cow. The story originated as a rumor in the Richland Beacon, and its location and truth were disputed by residents of the parish ward it named.

According to the Richland Beacon, which hedged its account with "if reports are true" and "it is said," a Black man was caught in the woods in the act of butchering a cow in the 5th ward of Morehouse parish. The men who detected him reportedly cut a small hole in the cow, removed its entrails, put him in the cavity and sewed up the hole, leaving only his head out. The item said he struggled to keep crows from picking at his eyes and was "almost completely exhausted" when two Black men found and released him. Neither the man nor the men who punished him were named, and no date was given.

Two weeks after reprinting the story, the Morehouse Clarion reported that several "reliable citizens" of the 5th ward had asked it to deny the charge. They did not condemn the punishment but protested "against the accusation of cow-stealing in their ward," and the Clarion retorted that Richland parish was "doubtless the scene of action." A correspondent of the Cotton Plant went further, calling the item a slander and demanding the name of its author.

In reply, the Beacon described its paragraph as a rumor that had been talked about in Rayville for a week or more and declined to name its sources. No arrest, inquest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The story circulated only in Louisiana white papers, which treated it as a curiosity. The Beacon credited the perpetrators with "the discovery of a new and original mode of punishing a cow thief," and the Morehouse Clarion reprinted the item on 2 September, saying it did not "by any means doubt its truth." The Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge carried it the next day in a column of state items, beside a report of two Black prisoners taken from the Monroe jail and hanged.

The dispute that followed concerned the reputation of the ward rather than the treatment of the man. The Clarion punned on a "bovine tragedy" and a "cow-PITAL mode of punishment," while the Beacon said it had thought it was adding "a small mite to the general stock of scientific knowledge."

The Beacon placed the incident in the 5th ward of Morehouse parish, whereas residents of that ward denied it and the Clarion pointed to Richland parish. The Clarion's later paraphrase also said the man was released by "some parties passing by" and tormented by buzzards, rather than freed by two Black men after fending off crows.

bases: Unnamed 'parties' were said to have seized a Black man caught butchering a cow and sewn him inside its carcass as punishment, with no killing or threat to kill reported (A1, A2).

All accounts derive from one Richland Beacon item that itself rested on talk in Rayville (A2, A4); citizens of the named ward denied it happened there and a Cotton Plant correspondent called it a slander (A3, A4).

accounts.label: Richland Beacon item (rumor)
accounts.gist: Hedged with 'if reports are true' and 'it is said': parties in the 5th ward of Morehouse caught a Black man butchering a cow in the woods, sewed him into the carcass with his head out, and two Black men later released him exhausted.

accounts.label: Fifth-ward citizens
accounts.gist: Several reliable citizens denied that cow-stealing occurred in their ward and said the Beacon was misinformed about where it happened, though they did not condemn the punishment.

accounts.label: Cotton Plant correspondent
accounts.gist: As described by the Beacon, the correspondent called the item a slander and demanded its author.

accounts.label: Richland Beacon defense
accounts.gist: The Beacon said it had printed a rumor that every man in Rayville had heard for a week or more, from about twenty people talking and laughing about it, and would not name sources.

framing.detail: The Beacon item credited the perpetrators with 'the discovery of a new and original mode of punishing a cow thief' and later called its paragraph a contribution to 'scientific knowledge'.
The Morehouse Clarion reprinted the item saying it did not doubt its truth; the Louisiana Capitolian ran it in a column of state items.
The Clarion's follow-up joked about a 'bovine tragedy' and a 'cow-PITAL mode of punishment', defending the ward's name rather than questioning the punishment.

versions.value: Not the 5th ward; Richland parish 'doubtless the scene of action'

conflicts.note: The Morehouse denial and the Clarion's Richland suggestion are partly jocular; the Beacon (Richland parish) maintained that it reported a rumor about Morehouse.
